title: Nothing is ever out of place.
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach's main teaching emphasizes the importance of embracing the paradoxical nature of life, where darkness and light are intertwined aspects of our experiences. By letting go of binary thinking and moral judgment, we can find freedom from trying to change or judge ourselves based on past events, and instead discover our true nature by being present with the world as it is. This includes accepting that karma is simply an unfolding of causes and conditions, rather than good or bad, allowing us to tap into the universal energy that points towards our own light, even in its darkest moments.

sentences.text: **Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Good evening everyone.
I feel very fortunate to be here with you all tonight.
The clouds are coming in, but I was thinking it's a perfect night of lengthening and warmth to give a talk like this.
First I want to thank you all for welcoming me so warmly to Red Cedar Zen Center.
For those of you who may be newer tonight, I appeared suddenly around the first of the year, and this is my first opportunity to introduce myself to you formally.

When I was thinking about what to talk about, I considered a variety of topics, whether to do this as a way-seeking mind talk so you'd actually get a chance to know this person a little bit, or to do it as a straight-up dharma talk.
So I'm going to do some of both.
It's a natural, because the topic I'm going to talk about is a kind of way-seeking mind talk.
Another way to talk about way-seeking mind is to call it bodhicitta.
Bodhicitta, many of you know, is the light, the part of you that is seeking truth, seeking to know your true self.
It's part of what got us all to show up here and come through the door.
So I'm going to talk about my version of that.
When you listen to this talk, I'll be speaking about the particulars of my life, but they're also the particulars of your lives.
I just don't know those particulars.
So when you listen, please listen out of meditation, out of your zazen, and welcome in your own story, welcome in your own experience as you hear it reflected in my words.
Although you'll hear about the particulars of my life, that's really not what's so important, except that it's my introduction to you.
Another way of saying bodhicitta: Suzuki Roshi, the founder of our lineage here and also my teacher's teacher, would call it the inmost request, that yearning you have to know your true self.
Sometimes we've spoken of it as our inner gold, or the jewel that's sewn inside your robe that you don't even know you're carrying, your fortune.
But I don't think it's exactly like those things.
I think more of how Dogen talks about this inmost request, or bodhicitta, in the fascicle Bucho, or called Buddha nature.
In Buddha nature he makes the radical, radical turning where he says, that's not something you have.
In a way it's not something you can find or misplace.
It's something that we are.
We're all made up of this enlightenment.
We're all made up of this light.
That's our true nature.
It may not always seem that way.
It certainly doesn't always seem that way to me.
There was a time when I would have thought that was ridiculous, because what I was looking for was to find the jewel inside the robe somewhere, the magic that would turn my life.
Maybe that's what brings us inside the door here.
Another way to talk about it is Master Ummon's comments in the 86th case of the Blue Cliff Record.
We've talked about Unmen a number of times here recently, so it's a natural to invoke this, probably the most prolific of the Chinese Tang masters that we read stories from.
It's a wonderful story that I've been chewing on for years now, and as I was preparing for this I thought I understood it a little bit differently.
I should say this talk actually has two titles.
The first one is "Nothing Is Ever Out of Place," which may seem totally different from "Everyone Has Their Own Life, Their Own Light."
So Master Unmen says everyone has a light.
When you look at it you don't see it, and it's dark and dim.
What is everyone's light?
I'd add, can you see it?
Can you know it?
How do you know it?
How does it reveal itself to you?
Unmen answered his students, who were sitting around befuddled by what he asked.
He said to them, "The kitchen pantry and the main gate."
What a funny answer that is.
He also said, "A good thing isn't as good as nothing."
A good thing isn't as good as nothing.
So you may have some idea about this light, but it's not as good as nothing.
We think we know something that we're seeking after, that jewel we're going to find to make it all right, but actually it's dark, dark and dim.
When we think we've found it, we've missed it entirely.
How is that jewel revealed to us?
Can we do that all by ourselves?
And what is that path?
Dogen says in Genjokoan, to study the self is to forget the self.
To forget the self is to be one of the myriad things.
So it's most important that we study the self.
It's most important that we look for this jewel.
But you'll be surprised how you find it.
Florence Caplow and Sue Moon, who are students of Norman's, wrote a book called The Hidden Lamp, which is a collection of women's stories.
I would imagine a number of you here have read it and even heard them speak about it.
One of those koans was written by my first teacher, Seisho Maylie Scott.
In that story a very earnest student comes up to her and says, "This crippling loneliness is preventing me from reaching my true self.
I can neither shake it nor live with it.
Can you give me a turning word?"
And she turned, in her New England way, a few words and said to the student, "Don't think anything is ever out of place."
And she walked away.
Now, I was that student, and I have to say I felt like a bucket of cold water had been dumped on me.
What could she possibly mean, that the way in which I had been suffering, for a good portion of my life to that point, that nothing could be out of place with that?
In some ways even that interlude was out of place.
I met her when I was seeking a teacher.
I quit my job and signed up on a whim to do a Buddhist training program that it turned out she was the mentor for.
When I met her my first thought was that she couldn't possibly be my teacher, but I guess I'll do the program anyway.
Sometimes we don't know, huh, where the light shines from.
I had had some inclination of what she meant.
I didn't have it in a personal way, but not long before that I had sat a 30-day silent Vipassana retreat.
Those of you who sit that style know that you sit day in and day out with nothing but your mind.
There's very little interaction with other people.
This was a 30-day retreat that had no teachers, so I really was all by myself without any of the forms or structures that we're familiar with in Zen.
You get very quiet and collected, and you really see how the workings of mind unfold in that kind of setting.
At one point I was walking down the hallway of the old former nunnery in southern England where I was, and there was a little crack in the world.
I suddenly understood in that moment that the way things were was exactly as they were meant to be.
We were in the middle of the first Iraq war at that point in time.
There was a lot in the news about bombs falling and destroying.
Things that are now so commonplace in our experience were not quite as commonplace then.
But the destruction and the war and the lives lost and the images, I suddenly understood that there was a natural unfolding of events, and that there was nothing out of place in that.
Now, if I time this right, there will be time for question and answer, and that may be provocative to you.
It certainly is a provocative thought, in some ways, to imagine that it's really in a certain way all right, meaning there's nothing unexpected.
There's nothing that could be different, given the conditions of the moment, for things to be the way they were.

I'm not saying they're not tragic, unskillful, but before I could say that they're wrong or immoral I have to understand that that's a personal compass, or the compass of a particular culture and time.
For a moment I understood clearly that it wasn't.
The thing is that karma itself is amoral.
Karma doesn't judge good and bad.
It just is what it is, the unfolding of causes and conditions as they are, the unfolding of causes and conditions that bring us to this moment as they are.
It's just that we can't see it entirely that way.
They don't unfold in a linear way.
We don't know all the circumstances.
We can't.
We don't even have our own consciousness, much less could we for world events or events that involve so many different factors.
That's true in our lives too.
It's also that it's not personal.
Events that happen aren't personal.

A brick, when it falls on our head, isn't falling on our head because we beat up our brother when we were eight, or because we happened to be careless with something we did earlier in the day, or because it's time for us to wake up.
It's really none of those things.
Maybe it means we need to pay attention a little bit better, but maybe it doesn't.
It's just that not everything is all about us.
So the causes and conditions that come together in this moment manifest themselves completely as they are, unconditioned.
Now, we study the Heart Sutra.
The Heart Sutra tells us about the impermanence and non-dependent nature of things, of our senses, of our perceptions, of our thoughts.
The Lankavatara Sutra tells us the same thing about karma.
The causes and conditions are empty in and of themselves.
They appear, they disappear.
They're freestanding.
This moment is freestanding.
So of course our intention, our precept practice, our right action, all of those matter.
They matter to the way we manifest our lives, but in their actual actions, the actual way they manifest for our own personal life, we don't expect anything from them.
They just show up as they are.
We just offer it up.
So that's my own story, Maylie's comment to me.
We all have these stories.
We all have these ideas where we don't think it's right, where the way it was shouldn't have been the way it was.
Sometimes that's subtle.
In my case, I'm adopted.
I should have been raised by other people.
I was an only child.
My parents were the ones who were far away from everyone else in their family.
I was alone.
That shouldn't have been.
I, like everyone else, was meant to be a part of something closer knit.
At least I really felt that.
I felt like something deep was missing as a result of that, and it seemed perfectly out of place.
The suffering seemed uniquely personal.
So when Maylie said to me, nothing is ever out of place, I had enough experience and trust in her that I had to ask that question.
What could that possibly mean?
How could this be exactly the right place that it is?
How could this yearning I have for being whole actually be manifest out of these circumstances?
Your yearning to be whole is manifest exactly out of your circumstances, no matter what they are.
Like the teenage girl who sat on the sofa in her living room at night and cried to touch the stars, there was a looking to touch that which was so far away, to find it inside of myself.
Nothing is ever out of place.
What could that mean?
It's a request for us to accept our lives exactly as they are.
These events that happened, they just were.
They weren't personal, based out of good or bad.
They were people doing their actions in the best way that they could, manifesting themselves out of their own causes and conditions in their life that came forward in this moment.
And it happened to land on, it happened to be like this for this person who is her own constitution of personality and events.
Just like each of you in your lives, and whatever brought you here and whatever your circumstances are, it just was what it was.
This is called radical acceptance.
Nothing is ever out of place.
It just is what it is.
How do I meet it?
How do I meet it?
The events of the past hold no moral or personal favor or grudge against me.
If I see them with rosy glasses or if I see them in smoky glasses, they're still distorted.
They're still glasses of the time.
They're not present here except in the way in which I actualize them.
They're not running this life now.
So I turned the channel and stopped saying "nobody loves me" anymore and just decided to continue to explore who this person really was.
Some years later, I want to say this is a journey of a lifetime.
The ways in which we create ourselves, in some ways this is very coarse, what I'm describing to you.
This idea of being lonely and separate in a certain way is a very gross experience of feelings not so digested from an early life.
But as time goes on, you'll find that there are finer and finer ways in which you create a self, and the self is supposed to be a certain way.
For example, how did I possibly get up here to Bellingham from the Bay Area, where I'd lived for over 30 years?
I'd been a physician there.
I served the community.
I worked for the poor.
How could it be that I could no longer afford to live there?
Didn't I deserve something better for my good work?
Times change.
The world is different.
Nothing's out of place.
You see, I can smile now, but a year and a half ago that wasn't so easy for a while.
That dissonance between who I thought I was and what my life was supposed to be about and what had happened.
Finer and finer we dissect this down and we see ourselves more clearly.
For many years, I thought I'd only understand this jewel that I am, that you are, that we are, if I could resolve some aspects of my difficult personality.
Somehow they were a moral failing that I had to get over.
Got 10 minutes?
A moral failing that I had to get over.
And then, by real great luck, I was able to get information about my birth mother, who had died.
A friend of hers had a biography that her husband had written, with pictures of my birth mother from the time she was a child and stories about who she was as a person.
I have to say I'm a carbon copy, including all the difficult personality traits.
They were in that woman.
I could see it in her face.
In some miraculous way, it set me free.
It was just the way it was.
It was not something that therapy was going to make go away.
It was not a moral failing on my part.
It was just the particular tune that this life plays.
It's just the music of this life, and it's up to me to dance with it.
To dance with it, like it is for all of us.
So in a funny way, that accepting, it's a handful of twos and threes.
How am I going to play this out?
That accepting gives so much more freedom.
It is just what it is.
So what?
I'm free now to be who I am.
I don't need to try and be someone that I'm not.
In that way, the light comes forward, because the light is our own natural essence.
You're open to the reality of who you really are, and you can engage with all of what life is.
There is no fear.
There's a curiosity and an openness to life, in the way that Kosho Uchiyama talks about life.
Big life.
Big life is the flow of what happens between all of us.
It's the way Indra's net moves, Indra's net that we're all connected to, like little points where the crossings of the net meet.
There's one little movement and everything moves together in some wonderful way.
You're open to be a part of that motion, part of that fluidity and that energy.
So what is that for you?
Who is it that sits here really?
There's nothing missing.
Ummon says when you look for your light, it's dark, dark.
It's not how you expect it to be.
It's not who you expect it to be.
It's a bit of a mystery revealing itself moment after moment after moment, in the way that causes and conditions just appear over and over again, and there's total freedom to be within that.
That is the darkness.
Front and back foot opposing one another.
The light and the darkness.
Not just the relative and the absolute, but that of our life.
Stepping deep down in and not touching bottom.
You know how it is when you're like that in the water and you just float.
There's a part two to this, but maybe that will be another talk sometime.
So, was that light mine or theirs?
Was it my mother's?
Can you tell?
Can you see for yourself?
It's on the main gate.
It's in the kitchen pantry.
No one holds it for you, but the whole universe is pointing right at it.
So I think we have a few minutes for questions.
At my old temple, Berkeley Zen Center, that was always the best part of a talk, being able to say something about what came up for you.
It might be a question or it might be your own experience.
This is being recorded, so if you'd like me to turn this off so your comment or question isn't heard, just let me know and I'm happy to do that.
Thank you very much for listening.
Yes, Connie?
**Participant:** It always seems to me like it's easy to say, accept things as they are, when we're sitting here in this beautiful, peaceful darn hall.
What about the people who are sitting in refugee camps, or sitting under bombs that are dropping, that this country is throwing at other nations?
Is that okay?
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Yes, it is.
That's always something that comes up for me.
It's very difficult.
I'm so glad that you asked that.
I think that's really a key question here.
In a certain way, it's not that it's okay from a moral or right or wrong standpoint.
It is that it is, and when you see it for what it is, you have more clarity about what the response is.
When one's own idea is that it shouldn't be this way, or it's wrong, or those people are doing it, or I'm helpless in this because it's so big, it's not possible to do anything.
So first I say sit with them in your meditation, in your walking prayers, when you say your prayers or make your chants.
Be with them.
Be with them and evoke your sincere desire to be of use in some way, and trust the impulse that comes out of it.
Yes, Alison?
**Participant:** In saying that each person has their own light, and then in saying how dim those lights are, would you rephrase that?
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Yeah.
So I think the dim, in my understanding now, is looking for it to be something in particular.
The dim is expecting it to be bright and shiny instead of everything that we are.
Instead of seeing that the delusive, the confused, the difficult, the whatever that we each have within ourselves, in our action, is also part of that light.
What do you say?
Yes.
That's a big decision.
See, it's dim-dim.
Anyone else?
**Participant:** I appreciate what you have to say.
It was very moving.
